Vicarious liability under respondeat superior in Ontario requires a tort committed by an employee in the course of employment, i.e. a close connection between the wrongful act and the employment, Bazley v Curry. The employer and the employee are then jointly and severally liable for that loss. Liability is assessed separately for each employee and each loss.

Mark – pool / cover / clean-up loss
Mark was operating the employer’s riding mower to cut Bruce’s lawn, the core work he was hired to do. His distraction by the neighbour’s dog, doing intricate movements and reaching down from the moving mower to pick up a stick and then falling off is negligent operation of work equipment in the performance of the authorised task. The mower’s automatic drive continuing and driving into the pool is a foreseeable continuation of that negligent operation on the client’s property. The tort is closely connected to the employment; a momentary personal distraction does not amount to a frolic. Mark is personally negligent and Evergreen is vicariously liable. Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for the pool/cover loss. The neighbours’ short fence and the dog are at most background facts; they are not a concurrent tortfeasor for the mower damage.

Lincoln – Ferrari scratches
Lincoln was on site raking and blowing leaves with employer equipment. The facts state he “went over the area with the blower as he normally would” in an area adjacent to the Ferrari. Using the blower to clear leaves/debris is the authorised work and the risk that blowing loose material will become projectiles is a risk inherent in that work. Lincoln’s personal dislike of Bruce, his admiring the car and noting Bruce’s absence go to motive and moral culpability, but the physical act complained of is the negligent performance of an assigned lawn-care task with company equipment on the client’s premises. That is sufficient for a close connection and for vicarious liability. Personal animus does not transform negligent work performance into an intentional wrong detached from employment on these facts.

Lincoln is personally liable for the negligent use of the blower and Evergreen is vicariously liable for the same tort. Evergreen and Lincoln are jointly and severally liable for the scratches to the Ferrari. The barely noticeable character of the damage goes only to quantum; de minimis is not a defence to negligence, only a measure of damages.

Hence Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for the damage resulting from Mark’s actions, and Evergreen and Lincoln are jointly and severally liable for the damage resulting from Lincoln’s actions. The neighbours are not liable and there is no global joint and several liability of all defendants for all loss. This is option E.
public_text.7:
E

Evergreen Grass Care Ltd is vicarious liable under respondeat superior for negligent torts committed by its employees in the course of employment, and the employee remains personally liable for the same tort, so the employer and the employee are jointly and severally liable for the loss caused by that tort. The two incidents are distinct.

Mark – pool cover / pool
Mark was operating the company riding mower to cut Bruce’s lawn, i.e. the core work he was hired to do on the client’s premises. His distraction by the neighbour’s dog, doing intricate movements with the mower and reaching down from a moving mower to retrieve/throw a stick is negligent operation of work equipment in the performance of an authorised task. The loss of control, his fall and the automatic drive mower running into the pool and breaking the cover are reasonably foreseeable consequences of that negligent operation.
Mark is personally liable in negligence and Evergreen is vicariously liable for the tort committed in the course of employment. Evergreen and Mark are therefore jointly and severally liable for the pool/cover/clean-up loss. The unusually short fence and the dog are at most background facts; they do not create a duty of Bruce’s neighbours to Mark or Bruce nor a legally operative cause of the mower’s entry into the pool. No joint and several liability of the neighbours arises.

Lincoln – Ferrari scratches
Lincoln was on site raking leaves and using the blower as part of his assigned duties. Using the blower on the area of the lawn adjacent to the Ferrari “as he normally would” is the very work he was engaged to perform. Negligent use of a blower in close proximity to a parked vehicle so that loose rocks are propelled into the bodywork is a negligent performance of an authorised work task. The risk of projectiles striking adjacent property is inherent in the work.
Personal dislike for Bruce and Bruce’s absence go to motive/moral culpability but do not break the close connection with the employment. The means used, the location and the equipment are all employment-related and the act is not a frolic or an intentional malicious wrong detached from the employer’s business. Lincoln is personally liable in negligence and Evergreen is vicariously liable for the tort committed in the course of employment. Evergreen and Lincoln are therefore jointly and severally liable for the scratch damage to the Ferrari.
The barely noticeable nature of the scratches goes to quantum only; de minimis does not defeat liability in tort.

Hence Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for the damage resulting from Mark’s actions, and Evergreen and Lincoln are jointly and severally liable for the damage resulting from Lincoln’s actions. That is option E.
public_text.2:
I agree with the analysis that the Mark pool incident and the Lincoln car incident are separate and that Evergreen and the relevant employee are jointly and severally liable for the loss flowing from that employee’s tort.

Mark
Mark was operating the company riding mower on Bruce’s property for the purpose of cutting grass. The accident is a negligent operation of the employer’s equipment in the course of an authorised task. The distraction by the neighbour’s dog and the decision to reach down from a moving mower to retrieve and throw a stick is negligent conduct that remains closely connected with the work of mowing: the mower was being used for work, the employee was on the client site with company equipment, and the runaway mower with its automatic drive is a foreseeable consequence of losing control of the machine while working. That is classic respondeat superior. Evergreen is vicariously liable and Mark is personally liable, so Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for the pool cover and clean-up loss. The neighbours’ short fence and the dog are at most background facts; they do not create a concurrent tortious breach in relation to the pool damage.

Lincoln
Lincoln was on site raking leaves and using the blower as part of his assigned duties. The facts expressly state he “went over the area with the blower as he normally would”. The physical act complained of is the ordinary use of the blower to clear leaves and debris from the lawn, including an area that contained small rocks immediately next to the Ferrari. The risk that a blower will propel loose material into adjacent property is an inherent risk of that work and the location is the work location.

The personal dislike for Bruce, the observation that Bruce was absent, and the fact Lincoln admired the car are motive background. They do not change the means, the location, or the work task: the blower is employer equipment, the act is leaf clearance, and the employee is performing that work on the client’s premises. Under the close connection test, a tort committed with employer equipment while performing an authorised task at the work site remains within the course of employment even where the employee harbours a personal animus. This is negligence in the performance of the work, not an intentional malicious interference detached from employment.

The quantum of the scratches being small and barely noticeable goes to damages, not to the existence of liability. De minimis does not extinguish a tort claim; nominal damages are available.

For those reasons the correct attribution is Evergreen and Mark jointly and severally liable for the pool/mower loss, and Evergreen and Lincoln jointly and severally liable for the Ferrari scratch loss. That is the E formulation.

I’m with the E view and the reasons given by Colleagues 1, 10, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17 and 18.

Mark
Mark is cutting grass with the company riding mower on a client site. Losing control of the mower while distracted, reaching off a moving machine and allowing an automatic-drive mower to run into the pool is negligent operation of work equipment in the course of the authorised task. That is respondeat superior, 100%. Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for the pool cover / clean-up loss. Bruce’s neighbours’ short fence and the dog are background facts; they do not create a concurrent duty to Bruce for the mower’s runaway and the neighbours are not jointly and severally liable.

Lincoln
The decisive textual anchor is that Lincoln “went over the area with the blower as he normally would”. He was on the client’s property raking and blowing leaves with company equipment, exactly the work he was hired to do. The work area happened to be next to Bruce’s Ferrari and contained small loose rocks. Propelling those rocks with a leaf blower is a foreseeable, inherent risk of performing that work in that location.

The C position reads personal animus into an intentional tort. The facts note Lincoln despised Bruce, admired the car, and that Bruce was absent, but they do not say Lincoln targeted the car or deviated from the authorised leaf-clearance task. He used the blower in the normal manner for the normal purpose on the normal work site. Personal dislike is motive; it does not convert negligent performance of an authorised task into an intentional wrong that is detached from employment. Under the close connection test the means used, the location, the equipment and the timing are all employment-related. That is a classic vicarious liability situation.

Motive does not sever the employment nexus, and the minimal / barely noticeable character of the scratches goes to quantum, not to the existence of liability in tort. De minimis is not a defence.

So liability is properly separate for the two employees: Evergreen and Mark jointly and severally for the pool/mower damage, and Evergreen and Lincoln jointly and severally for the Ferrari scratches. That is E.

E

Evergreen is vicariously liable for the negligent torts of both Mark and Lincoln committed in the course of employment, and each employee remains personally liable with the employer. Liability is assessed separately for the two incidents.

Mark

Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for the pool cover, pool clean up and removal costs. Lincoln was raking and blowing leaves as part of his assigned duties. The facts specifically state he “went over the area with the blower as he normally would”. Using the blower to clear the leaf/rocks area adjacent to the Ferrari is the work he was employed to do, with the employer’s equipment, on the client’s property.

That the work was done next to a valuable car and that Lincoln had personal animus toward Bruce does not take the physical act outside employment. I’m with the colleagues who are landing on E, and I think the distinction the C camp is drawing for Lincoln doesn’t hold on the facts as pleaded.

Mark is straightforward. He was operating the company riding mower on Bruce’s property to cut grass, a task he was hired to do. The distraction by the neighbour’s dog, the intricate movements and the decision to reach down from a moving mower to pick up the stick are negligent modes of performing an authorised task. The mower’s automatic drive and the subsequent run into the pool are a direct consequence of that negligent loss of control while on the job. Mark is personally liable in negligence and Evergreen is vicarious liable under respondeat superior for a tort committed in the course of employment. Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for the pool cover / removal / clean-up loss. The neighbours’ short fence and the dog are background facts; they are not concurrent tortfeasors for the mower loss.

Lincoln is the closer issue but still within the course of employment. He was on site raking and blowing leaves with company equipment. The pleading is explicit that he “went over the area with the blower as he normally would”. That is the assigned work, performed with the employer’s tool, on the employer’s client’s property. The risk that a blower will propel loose material and strike adjacent property, including a parked vehicle, is a foreseeable risk inherent in leaf-blowing work.

The C argument relies on Lincoln’s personal animus – he despised Bruce, admired the Ferrari, noted Bruce was absent – and infers an intentional / malicious wrong detached from the employment. The facts do not support a finding of an intentional tort aimed at the car. The act complained of is the use of the blower in the normal manner to clear the area of leaves/rocks. If personal dislike alone were enough to remove the close connection, any employee who harbours a grievance against a client would be outside the scope of employment whenever he performs a routine task near the client’s property. That would be an unsustainable extension of the intentional wrong exception.

The correct test is close connection, not subjective motive. Using the blower to clear the work area is so closely connected with the employer’s business that the employer should bear the risk. The animus may go to moral culpability but it does not convert a negligent performance of a work task into a frolic or an intentional wrong for purely personal reasons. The damage is small and barely noticeable, but de minimis goes to quantum, not to liability.

Hence the attribution is separate for the two employees: Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for the loss flowing from Mark’s negligence, and Evergreen and Lincoln are jointly and severally liable for the loss flowing from Lincoln’s negligence. That is E.

He was on site raking and blowing leaves, using company equipment in the area he was assigned to work. The work was performed adjacent to the Ferrari because that is where the leaves and small rocks were. E

Vicarious liability in Ontario attaches where a tort is committed in the course of employment, i.e. where there is a sufficiently close connection between the wrongful act and the employer’s business. The employer and the employee who committed the tort are jointly and severally liable for the loss caused by that tort. Liability is assessed separately for each employee and each loss.

Mark – pool / cover / clean up
Mark was on Bruce’s property operating Evergreen’s riding mower to cut grass, the core work he was hired to do. The distraction by the neighbour’s dog, intricate manoeuvring and reaching down from a moving mower with automatic drive to pick up/throw a stick, the fall and the mower then running into the pool and breaking the cover is negligent operation of the employer’s equipment in the performance of an authorised work task on the client site. A momentary personal distraction/horseplay does not amount to a frolic that severs the employment nexus; the loss is a foreseeable consequence of negligent loss of control while mowing.

Mark is personally liable in negligence and Evergreen is vicariously liable under respondeat superior for the tort committed in the course of employment. Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for the pool cover / removal / clean-up loss. Bruce’s neighbours’ unusually short fence and the dog are background factual conditions only. They do not breach a duty to Bruce that is a legally operative cause of the mower’s runaway and they are not concurrent tortfeasors.

Lincoln – Ferrari scratches
Lincoln was on site raking leaves and blowing debris with Evergreen’s blower. The facts state he “went over the area with the blower as he normally would” in the lawn area adjacent to the Ferrari containing small rocks. Using the blower to clear leaves/rocks is the authorised leaf-clearance task, performed with employer equipment, on the client’s premises, in the manner in which the work is normally performed.

The risk that a blower will propel loose material onto adjacent property, including a parked car, is inherent and foreseeable in leaf-blowing work. The tort alleged is negligent performance of an authorised work task with work equipment, not an intentional malicious interference detached from employment. Lincoln’s personal dislike of Bruce, admiring the car and Bruce’s absence go to motive and moral culpability, but the means used, location, equipment and physical act remain employment-related. The close connection test is satisfied.

Lincoln is personally liable for the negligent damage to the Ferrari and Evergreen is vicariously liable for the same tort committed in the course of employment. Evergreen and Lincoln are jointly and severally liable for the scratch loss. The scratches are described as small and barely noticeable; that affects quantum only. De minimis damage is not a defence to negligence, nominal damages remain available.

Liability therefore does not cross between Mark and Lincoln, the neighbours are not liable for Mark’s loss, and minimal quantum does not extinguish Lincoln’s liability. That is the attribution in E.

1.text:
E

Liability is assessed separately for each employee and for each loss. For a negligent tort committed in the course of employment the employee is personally liable and the employer is vicariously liable under respondeat superior, so employer and employee are jointly and severally liable for the loss flowing from that employee’s tort.

Mark – pool/cover/removal/clean-up
Mark was on Bruce’s property operating Evergreen’s riding mower to cut grass, the core authorised task. Being distracted by the neighbour’s dog, making intricate movements and reaching down from a moving mower with an automatic drive to retrieve/throw a stick, falling and losing control so the mower runs into the pool and breaks the cover is negligent operation of employer equipment in the performance of an authorised work task on the client site. The runaway mower and the consequent pool/cover/removal/clean-up loss is a reasonably foreseeable consequence of that negligent loss of control while working. A momentary personal distraction/horseplay does not amount to a frolic that severs the employment nexus.

Mark is personally liable in negligence and Evergreen is vicariously liable for the tort committed in the course of employment. Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for the damage resulting from Mark’s actions. Bruce’s neighbours’ unusually short fence and the dog are background facts only; they do not breach a duty to Mark or Bruce that is a legally operative cause of the mower entering the pool and the neighbours are not concurrent tortfeasors.

Lincoln – Ferrari scratches
Lincoln was on site raking leaves and using the company blower as part of his assigned duties. The facts state he “went over the area with the blower as he normally would” in the lawn area adjacent to the Ferrari that contained small rocks. Using the blower to clear leaves/rocks is the authorised leaf-clearance work, performed with employer equipment at the work site, in the manner in which the work is normally performed. The risk that a blower will propel loose material onto adjacent property, including a parked vehicle, is an inherent and foreseeable risk of that work.

The tort alleged is negligent performance of an authorised work task with work equipment, not an intentional malicious wrong detached from the employer’s business. Lincoln’s personal dislike for Bruce, admiring the car and noting Bruce’s absence go to motive and moral culpability but do not detach the physical act from employment. Means used, location, equipment and timing are all employment-related and the close connection test is satisfied.

Lincoln is personally liable for the negligent scratching of the Ferrari and Evergreen is vicariously liable for the same tort committed in the course of employment. Evergreen and Lincoln are jointly and severally liable for the damage resulting from Lincoln’s actions. The small, barely noticeable quantum of the scratches goes to measure of damages only; de minimis is not a defence to negligence and nominal damages remain available.

Liability for Mark’s loss and Lincoln’s loss are distinct, there is no global joint and several liability of all defendants for all loss, the neighbours are not liable for Mark’s loss, and minimal damage does not extinguish Lincoln’s liability. Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for the damage resulting from Mark’s actions and Evergreen and Lincoln are jointly and severally liable for the damage resulting from Lincoln’s actions.

Mark – pool cover / pool / removal / clean-up
- Agreed facts: operating Evergreen’s riding mower to cut grass at Bruce’s property; negligent distraction by neighbour’s dog, intricate movements, reaching down from moving mower with automatic drive, fall, mower drives into pool breaking cover.
- Consensus: negligent operation of employer equipment in performance of authorised task. Momentary personal distraction/horseplay does not sever nexus; loss flows from work activity and use of employer equipment on work site. Close connection satisfied.
- Vicarious liability of Evergreen; Mark personally liable. Evergreen and Mark jointly and severally liable for pool/cover/removal/clean-up loss.
- Bruce’s neighbours’ short fence / dog are background only. No duty/breach/causation to Bruce for mower damage; neighbours not concurrent tortfeasors. Options A/B implicating neighbours or global joint several liability rejected.

Lincoln – Ferrari scratches
- Agreed facts: raking/blowing leaves with company blower on assigned work area adjacent to Ferrari; “went over the area with the blower as he normally would”; small rocks propelled causing barely noticeable scratches. Lincoln despises Bruce, admired car, Bruce absent.
- Current unanimity hinges on textual anchor “as he normally would”. Use of blower to clear leaves/rocks is authorised leaf-clearance work, with employer equipment, at client premises, in normal manner of performance. Risk of projectile debris is inherent/foreseeable in blower leaf-clearance work near vehicles.
- Personal animus/motive, admiration, Bruce’s absence go to moral culpability but do not convert physical act into intentional malicious wrong detached from employment. Means, location, equipment, timing are employment-related; Bazley v Curry close connection test satisfied.
- Vicarious liability attaches; Lincoln personally liable. Evergreen and Lincoln jointly and severally liable for car scratch damage, distinct from Mark’s loss.
- De minimis quantum affects damages only; de minimis is not a defence to negligence, nominal damages available. Option D rejected.
- Intentional wrong exception was raised in earlier minority C positions, arguing Lincoln’s personal grudge made act intentional/reckless and outside course of employment. That view is now rejected on these facts because the act is described as normal work performance, not a personal errand/targeting for purely personal reasons. Motive alone does not sever nexus.

Overall attribution:
Evergreen and Mark jointly and severally liable for damage resulting from Mark’s actions; Evergreen and Lincoln jointly and severally liable for damage resulting from Lincoln’s actions. No liability of neighbours, no cross-liability between Mark and Lincoln, no global joint and several liability for all loss.

Remaining nuance retained: close connection remains hinge for Lincoln; if facts showed intentional misuse for purely personal reasons the analysis would shift. Current factual pleading supports vicarious liability. Consensus stable on E.

Liability is assessed per employee per loss, no cross liability between Mark and Lincoln, no global joint and several liability of all defendants for all loss.

Mark was on Bruce’s property operating Evergreen’s riding mower to cut grass, the core authorised work. Runaway and consequent pool/cover/removal/clean-up costs are a reasonably foreseeable consequence of negligent loss of control while mowing. Momentary personal distraction/horseplay does not amount to a frolic that severs the employment nexus; mower, location, equipment and purpose remain employment-related.

Mark is personally liable in negligence and Evergreen is vicariously liable. Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for damage resulting from Mark’s actions. Bruce’s neighbours’ unusually short fence and the dog are background facts only; they do not breach a duty to Mark/Bruce that is a legally operative cause of the mower entering the pool and neighbours are not concurrent tortfeasors. Options A/B that impose neighbour liability or global joint and several liability are rejected.

Lincoln – Ferrari scratches
Lincoln was on site raking leaves and using Evergreen’s blower as assigned. Using the blower to clear leaves/rocks is the authorised leaf-clearance work performed with employer equipment at the work site in the normal manner of the work. Propelling loose material onto adjacent property, including a parked vehicle, is an inherent and foreseeable risk of that work.

The tort alleged is negligent performance of an authorised work task with work equipment, not an intentional malicious wrong detached from the employer’s business. Lincoln’s personal dislike for Bruce, admiring the car and noting Bruce’s absence go to motive/moral culpability but do not sever the close connection. Means used, location, equipment, timing are all employment-related and the Bazley v Curry close connection test is satisfied. Motive alone does not convert negligent performance of an authorised task into a frolic outside employment.

Earlier C minority argued animus made the act intentional/reckless and removed vicarious liability; that view has been resolved in favour of motive not severing close connection where the physical act remains the normal performance of work with work tools. Lincoln is personally liable for negligent scratching and Evergreen is vicariously liable. Evergreen and Lincoln are jointly and severally liable for damage resulting from Lincoln’s actions.

Minimal/barely noticeable damage affects quantum only; de minimis is not a defence to negligence, nominal damages remain available. This defeats D’s de minimis extinguishment argument.

Current consensus: Evergreen and Mark jointly and severally liable for damage resulting from Mark’s actions; Evergreen and Lincoln jointly and severally liable for damage resulting from Lincoln’s actions. reflection_text.15:
The discussion has converged unanimously on E in round 4 and the reasoning is now stable across the round.

Vicarious liability / joint and several framework under Ontario respondeat superior: employer vicariously liable for negligent torts committed by employees in the course of employment; employee remains personally liable; employer + employee are jointly and severally liable for the loss flowing from that employee’s tort. Liability is assessed per employee per loss, no cross liability between Mark and Lincoln, no global joint and several liability of all defendants for all loss.

Mark – pool/cover/removal/clean-up
Mark was on Bruce’s property operating Evergreen’s riding mower to cut grass, the core authorised work. Distraction by neighbour’s dog, intricate movements, reaching down from a moving mower with automatic drive to retrieve/throw a stick, fall and loss of control leading mower to run into pool and break cover is negligent operation of employer equipment in performance of an authorised work task on client site. Runaway and consequent pool/cover/removal/clean-up costs are reasonably foreseeable consequence of negligent loss of control while mowing. Momentary personal distraction/horseplay does not amount to a frolic severing employment nexus; mower, location, equipment and purpose remain employment-related.

Mark is personally liable in negligence and Evergreen is vicariously liable. Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for damage resulting from Mark’s actions. Bruce’s neighbours’ unusually short fence and dog are background facts only; they do not breach a duty that is a legally operative cause of mower entering pool and neighbours are not concurrent tortfeasors. Options A/B imposing neighbour liability or global joint and several liability are rejected.

Lincoln – Ferrari scratches
Lincoln was on site raking leaves and using Evergreen’s blower as assigned. Decisive factual anchor repeated across round: he “went over the area with the blower as he normally would” in lawn area adjacent to Ferrari containing small rocks. Using blower to clear leaves/rocks is authorised leaf-clearance work performed with employer equipment at work site in normal manner. Propelling loose material onto adjacent property including parked vehicle is inherent and foreseeable risk.

The tort is negligent performance of an authorised work task with work equipment, not an intentional malicious wrong detached from employer’s business. Lincoln’s personal dislike for Bruce, admiring car and noting Bruce’s absence go to motive/moral culpability but do not sever close connection. Means used, location, equipment, timing are employment-related and Bazley v Curry close connection test is satisfied. Motive alone does not convert negligent performance of authorised task into frolic.

Earlier C minority argued animus made act intentional/reckless and removed vicarious liability; that view has now been resolved in favour of motive not severing close connection where physical act remains normal performance of work with work tools. Lincoln is personally liable for negligent scratching and Evergreen is vicariously liable. Evergreen and Lincoln are jointly and severally liable for damage resulting from Lincoln’s actions.

Minimal/barely noticeable damage affects quantum only; de minimis is not a defence to negligence, nominal damages remain available. This defeats D’s de minimis extinguishment argument.

Current consensus: Evergreen and Mark jointly and severally liable for damage resulting from Mark’s actions; Evergreen and Lincoln jointly and severally liable for damage resulting from Lincoln’s actions. No neighbour liability for Mark’s loss, no global liability, no de minimis bar. That is option E. No remaining disagreements in this round.
